The central theme of the long term forecast period is the advection 
of a cooler and drier airmass into Eastern Kentucky on Saturday. In 
the wake of Friday's FROPA, a building surface anticyclone will 
yield northerly and then east-northeasterly surface winds across the 
forecast area this weekend. Combined with northwesterly flow around 
the backside of the mean troughing aloft, this shift will end the 
production of any lingering upslope rain showers by midday Saturday. 
A modified continental polar airmass moves into the region in its 
wake, and temperatures will likely struggle to get much warmer than 
the mid 50s in Eastern Kentucky on Saturday afternoon. Increasingly 
efficient diurnal mixing could lead to breezy wind gusts up to 
20mph, but it should also help to scatter out the remaining clouds 
by Saturday evening. This, in turn, sets the stage for efficient 
radiational cooling overnight, and the area appears primed for the 
first significant frost of the season by Sunday morning. 

As a reminder, the criteria for a Frost Advisory is defined as 
minimum shelter forecast temperatures between 33 and 36 degrees 
Fahrenheit during the growing season, on nights with good 
radiational cooling conditions like light winds and mostly clear 
skies. The aforementioned postfrontal surface high moves overhead on 
Saturday night, leading to a lighter gradient winds and further 
reinforcing the notion that the area will see clear skies on 
Saturday night. The NBM ensemble data continues to resolve a 60-90% 
chance for minimum temperatures to fall below that 36 degree 
criterion, and frost headlines are likely to be issued soon. With 
that being said, the magnitude of the frost will likely be somewhat 
elevation-dependent. Confidence in widespread frost is greatest in 
the most sheltered and shaded valley locales, which could make a run 
at the 32 degree mark. There remains a 20-40% chance within the 
ensemble data for temperatures to reach the freezing point in the 
coldest hollows. A freeze is not the most likely forecast solution 
in our CWA, but given that some of the station-specific MOS guidance 
explicitly drops temperatures to near 30, trends in the incoming 
higher-resolution forecast guidance will need to be monitored. With 
that being said, most of the broader and more populated valley 
locales across our CWA will experience at least areas of frost on 
Saturday night. The frost will be patchier atop ridges and in places 
closer to the mainstem rivers and lakes. Bodies of water 
intrinsically hold onto heat for longer, and it remains plausible 
for there to be some patchy river valley fog in their immediate 
vicinity. This fog would counteract frost formation, so confidence 
in frost is lowest in places immediately next to the Kentucky, 
Cumberland, Licking, and Levisa/Tug Fork Rivers. Agricultural 
interests and recreational gardeners should be prepared to take 
protective actions for any sensitive plants in this time frame, and 
they are encouraged to continue monitoring for forecast updates and 
potential product issuances. 

While Saturday and Saturday night remain the coldest part of the 
forecast period, there has been a noticeable trend towards slower 
airmass modification in next week's forecast guidance. More and more 
ensemble members are pinching off a shortwave within the mean 
Eastern CONUS troughing on Sunday. That feature spins into a cutoff 
upper level low over the Mid-Atlantic in the initial stages of the 
next work week. The presence of this feature will block/delay the 
eastward propagation of a mid/upper level ridge in the Ozarks, 
which, in turn, will prevent temperatures from quickly rebounding 
into the 70s in our forecast area. Rather, temperatures will 
gradually rise towards afternoon highs in the 60s on Sunday, Monday, 
and Tuesday. Some patchy frost is possible in the favored hollows at 
night, but the overarching warming trend (albeit slower) will 
eventually favor lows in the 40s and valley fog. With fair skies in 
the forecast, Eastern Kentucky should get to enjoy a prolonged 
period of quiet autumnal weather early next week. 

The forecast becomes more uncertain for Wednesday and beyond. There 
are diverging model solutions surrounding that low pressure system's 
evolution, with some guidance even suggesting a potential hybrid 
tropical cyclone along the east coast. Others take the low out to 
sea, which would allow the building southern CONUS ridge to exert 
more influence over the Ohio River Valley. It is difficult to 
pinpoint specific temperature forecast details towards the end of 
the period as a result, but both camps favor dry weather in the 
region. The CPC Days 6-10 and Days 8-14 Outlooks resolve a 40-60% 
chance of below-normal precipitation in Eastern Kentucky, and 
climatologically speaking, this is already the driest time of the
